hints: Look closely at region X on the curve. What happens to the rate of reaction as temperature increases there?
Remember, a limiting factor is the one variable that is holding the rate back. Since temperature is the only thing being changed and the rate responds to it, what does that tell you?
walkthrough:
**Observe what is happening in region X**

Look at the left, rising part of the curve labelled region X. As temperature goes up, the rate of reaction goes up too.

That tells us the rate is responding to temperature in this region.

**Recall what temperature does to enzymes**

At lower temperatures, molecules have less kinetic energy. That means fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate, and fewer successful enzyme-substrate complexes per second.

Increasing temperature gives more kinetic energy, more frequent collisions, and a faster rate.

**Identify the limiting factor**

A limiting factor is the factor that is preventing the rate from being faster. If changing it changes the rate, it is limiting.

In region X, raising temperature raises the rate, so temperature is holding the rate back. It is limiting.

options.A: Substrate concentration was standardised and is not being changed, so it cannot explain why the rate rises when temperature rises.
options.B: Enzyme concentration was also standardised and kept constant, so it is not the variable controlling the rate in region X.
options.C: In region X the rate increases as temperature increases, showing low kinetic energy and low collision frequency are holding the rate back. Temperature is limiting.
options.D: At these lower temperatures the enzyme is not saturated, so there are plenty of empty active sites available. Lack of active sites is not what limits the rate.
